blocks.prompt: 8. A received message polynomial is \(P(x) = x^5 + x^3 + x + 1\) and a known error-detecting polynomial is \(g(x) = x + 1\). Find whether the received message is error-free using the remainder theorem.
blocks.explanation:
In error detection a message is sent so that its polynomial divides exactly by \(g(x)\); remainder 0 on arrival means no error was found.
We must decide: error-free or not.
Plan: write \(x + 1 = x - (-1)\), find the remainder \(P(-1)\); 0 means error-free, non-zero means an error.
steps:
Given: received message \(P(x) = x^5 + x^3 + x + 1\), error-detecting polynomial \(g(x) = x + 1\).
To find: whether the message is error-free.
Method: Remainder Theorem: the remainder on dividing \(P(x)\) by \(x - a\) is \(P(a)\). The message is error-free when this remainder is 0.

Find the value to use
\[x + 1 = x - (-1)\]
\[\Rightarrow a = -1\]
Why: The theorem is stated for \(x - a\), so \(x + 1\) gives \(a = -1\).

Work out \(P(-1)\)
\[P(-1) = (-1)^5 + (-1)^3 + (-1) + 1\]
\[= -1 - 1 - 1 + 1\]
\[= -2\]
Why: All the powers here (5, 3 and 1) are odd, so each gives \(-1\); only the constant \(+1\) stays positive.

Draw the conclusion
\[\text{Remainder} = -2 \neq 0\]
Why: \(g(x) = x + 1\) does not divide the received message exactly, so the message is not error-free: something changed during sending.

Check by synthetic division by \(x + 1\) (\(a = -1\))
Coefficients \(1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 1\) (zeros for the missing \(x^4\) and \(x^2\)):
\(1\); \(0 - 1 = -1\); \(1 + 1 = 2\); \(0 - 2 = -2\); \(1 + 2 = 3\); \(1 - 3 = -2\).
\[\text{Remainder} = -2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Missing powers must get a 0 coefficient, otherwise the columns shift. The division gives the same remainder \(-2\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the answer key (PDF 307) this question's answer is printed as entry 9, "Received message is not error-free, because remainder is non-zero", which agrees with our working. Entry 10 ("Code word is not valid, because \(x - 1\) is not a factor of \(C(x)\)") belongs to no printed question: there is no \(C(x)\) in this exercise.
